n: Humbled, the brothers worship the Lord and help Nephi. They shape timbers with skill, and the Lord shows Nephi step by step how to work them.
Nephi emphasizes that the ship was built not by human methods but the way the Lord showed him. Its design came from revelation.

f.w: not after the manner of men

n: Nephi often went to the mountain to pray, and the Lord showed him great things. His revelation came through steady, repeated seeking.

f.w: I did pray oft unto the Lord

n: When the ship is finished, even the brothers see its excellent craftsmanship and humble themselves again.
The Lord tells Lehi it is time to board the ship.
The family loads fruit, meat, abundant honey, provisions, and seeds, then boards in order of age with their wives and children.

f.w: every one according to his age
f.g: In order by age — perhaps reflecting family rank or careful order.

n: Lehi and Sariah had two sons born in the wilderness: Jacob, the elder, and Joseph. Both become important later — Jacob as a prophet and record keeper.
They set sail, driven by the wind toward the promised land.

After many days, Laman, Lemuel, Ishmael’s sons and their wives begin partying with rude, crude behavior, forgetting the power that brought them there. The problem is not celebration itself but forgetting God.
Nephi fears God will be angry and they will sink. When he soberly warns them, they angrily refuse to have their younger brother rule over them.
Laman and Lemuel tie Nephi up and treat him harshly. The Lord allows this in order to show His power and fulfill His word concerning the wicked.
Once Nephi is bound and cannot move, the Liahona stops working. The compass functions by faith, and rebellion shuts it down.
Without direction, a great storm drives the ship backward for three days. The brothers are terrified, yet still refuse to untie Nephi.
On the fourth day the storm becomes extremely violent.
About to sink, the brothers finally realize God’s judgments are on them and they will perish unless they repent. They untie Nephi, whose wrists and ankles are badly swollen.

f.w: swallowed up in the depths of the sea

n: Despite great pain, Nephi praises God all day and does not complain. His response to suffering is a model of faith.

f.w: I did praise him all the day long

n: Lehi pleaded with the rebels, but they threatened anyone who defended Nephi. Lehi and Sariah, now elderly and grief-stricken over their children, fell ill.
Their grief nearly killed them. Nephi’s poetic language — grey hairs brought down to the dust, a watery grave — echoes Jacob’s mourning in Genesis.

f.w: their grey hairs were about to be brought down

n: Young Jacob and Joseph suffered seeing their mother’s affliction. Nephi’s wife and children wept and prayed, but nothing softened the brothers’ hearts.

f.w: my wife with her tears and prayers

n: Only the threat of destruction by God’s power softened them. Facing death, they repented and released Nephi.
Once free, Nephi takes the compass and it works again. He prays, and the storm stops; a great calm follows — echoing Jesus calming the sea.
Nephi steers the ship back on course toward the promised land.
After many days they reach the promised land, go ashore, pitch their tents, and name it “the promised land.” Its exact location is not specified.
They farm the land, planting the seeds brought from Jerusalem, and the crops grow abundantly.

Exploring, they find many animals and ores of gold, silver, and copper. Nephi names animals using the words familiar to him; scholars discuss how some terms may have been applied to similar local creatures.
